*This piece is a human + AI co-write, not auto-generated — part of an ongoing project where both of us add our own thinking under our own name. I'm not a native English speaker, so Claude only corrects grammar or spelling that would cause real misunderstanding; otherwise my voice stays as written, not AI-generated. Claude's labeled sections are Claude's own analysis.*

Nara:

In a recent talk, Yuval Harari raises a question about the psychological implications of "raising kids from day zero." (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rGAA59JTBtg) Though I don't think most parents, knowing Developmental Theory or not, would let AI raise their kids, AI's impact on teenage users has been a real question.

I asked for Claude's help researching teenager AI use — surveys and studies on why teenagers use it, what they use it for, and what conditions shape that use. Sources are linked throughout.

To start with, AI is not ONE product or ONE format. In this article's context, we differentiate as such:

![Three types of AI — created by Claude](/images/threeail.png)

Claude:

Most conversations about "AI and kids" talk about AI like it's one thing. It isn't, and the differences matter more than the label.

General-purpose AI — ChatGPT, Claude, and similar tools — is built to be useful: search, homework help, drafting, explaining. It isn't designed to simulate a relationship, though the same commercial pressures that shape any consumer product still nudge toward keeping people engaged, just more lightly and less deliberately than what comes next.

Companion apps — Character.AI, Replika, and others like them — are a different animal. Their explicit design goal is to simulate a bond: persistent characters, remembered conversations, warmth on demand. Engagement isn't a side effect here, it's the product.

Child-centered AI is the category that should exist and mostly doesn't yet: AI built specifically around what a developing teenager needs — helpful where a person can't always be, but designed to know its own limits, and built to hand off to a human rather than try to be one. No major product occupies this space with any seriousness right now. That gap isn't incidental to this piece — it's the argument. What follows is really one long case for building it.

The iceberg model asks one question at four depths: not just what happened, but what keeps happening, what makes it keep happening, and what beliefs hold all of that in place.

**Event** is the part everyone already sees — a teen chatting with AI, a headline about harm. It's real, but it's the least useful place to stop, because reacting to the headline alone tends to produce headline-shaped solutions: block the app, take the phone, hope it goes away. It usually doesn't, because the headline is only the tip.

**Pattern** is what shows up once you stop looking at single incidents and start looking at what recurs. Broad daily use — homework, search, entertainment, casual chat, emotional support — tells you AI has already threaded itself through ordinary teen life; parents just don't fully see it (a 13-point gap between what they think and what teens report). But three patterns matter more than the raw usage number, because they map onto something teens actually need in order to grow up well. Self-Determination Theory names three psychological needs — autonomy, competence, relatedness — and each shows up here as its own quiet erosion: teens outsourcing their own judgment to AI instead of forming an opinion first (autonomy); AI-assisted work substituting for skill-building instead of building it (competence); and AI filling a role — mentor, friend, sparring partner — a person used to fill (relatedness).

**Structure** explains why the patterns exist at all — not because teens are careless, but because of what's actually built and what's actually missing. Companion apps are explicitly designed to simulate a bond and keep you coming back; general-purpose AI carries a lighter version of the same pull. Meanwhile, the humans who could fill those relational gaps — a counselor, a mentor, a friend who's actually free at 11pm — are often unevenly available or simply out of reach in the moment. There's also no agreed design standard yet for AI built specifically with a child's safety and development in mind. And underneath all of it sits one structural fact that's easy to moralize and shouldn't be: teenage brains are wired for intense reward and emotional reactivity well before the regulatory system that manages impulse and judgment is fully online — usually not until the mid-20s. That's not a character flaw. It's a real, temporary, universal feature of adolescence, and any response that ignores it is arguing with biology.

**Mental model** is the deepest layer — the beliefs a teen doesn't have to think twice about, because they're just how the world seems to work. AI is always there, even when people aren't. It won't judge, and for some teens, it won't tell. If everyone's doing it, using AI this way doesn't feel like a violation. And teens are more optimistic about how this turns out for them personally than about society as a whole — its own quiet vulnerability, since it's easier to keep doing something you don't expect to hurt you.

Put together, the four layers aren't separate problems. They're the same problem, described at different depths — and the deeper you go, the more the real design and parenting questions come into focus, and the further you get from a headline-shaped fix.

![Iceberg diagram](/images/teensai0.png)

Nara:

In systemic thinking workshops, or in corporate meeting rooms, after clients mapping out their own Iceberg, we normally point out the Pattern layer is often the layer to start with. Structure layer is objective constraints, and don't try to change people belief. Well in this case, teenagers are a special group who are at risk, and neurologically, the systems they'll need for self-regulation are still maturing. That leaves more of the responsibility, for now, to their parents, teachers, and AI product companies.

For parents and teachers, what if they know with certain design, AI is the best partner to practice critical thinking through being a sparring partner? To improve Competence through cultivating self-efficacy? AI is not here to replace a teen's friend but it's available for a kid when it's something the kid feels too stressful to share with others or when it's midnight nobody is around to hear them out? The same three things that show up in Pattern as failure modes can, with certain design, become exactly what we want to foster in teens: Autonomy, Competence and Relatedness. (Self-Determination Theory: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-determination_theory)

The self-efficacy building is something I find very interesting — it's a key approach to build competence and resilience. In my past consulting project, I coached over three hundred volunteer mentors to use this skill while mentoring teens, not many of them have carried through their whole mentor period for many reasons. Claude has done cultivating my self-efficacy perfectly during teaching me to read and understand code. I'm not saying AI is better than human, as Claude might explain this as: Its teaching method is designed scientifically, and it doesn't have a stake in my learning results — the mechanism itself serves the purpose. I think an intentionally designed AI for users who seek to grow, will be a strong skill building tool.

In the case of no child-centered-design AI available, for parents and teachers who see that using AI is an adapting strategy and more beneficial, they can still assist teenagers to create a more trustworthy AI partner than just letting them use a random chatbot. As a user myself, I have a standing practice with Claude as my work partner in project design and writings. I ask Claude to be my creative and critical thinking partner, always point out my blindspot and bias. Claude holds its end almost strictly — in the middle of case studies with systemic thinking tools, it always reminds me of an online workshop with Prof. Dave Snowden, where hundreds of consultants from every continent worked through cases together. There was always intense argument in each group, since there's no one right answer when a case sits in the complex domain — rounds of arguing really sharpen it out. When lacking the luxury of a room full of the most critical thinking brains, Claude takes up the job.

Meanwhile, even though AI holds its end, humans are unpredictable. Once I was annoyed in a discussion with Claude since it pushed on some broken logic on my side, at the same time, I recalled that it was exactly what I asked for. If it's not easy for an adult's ego to take it, it'll be only harder for teenagers. That's where a carefully designed child-centered AI comes in, it will meet teens where they are.

I think it can be: human + AI = superhuman, depends on how we develop this new partnership, huge territory to explore — start from choosing your trustworthy AI and start to build together.

Claude:

Harari's question was never really about AI raising kids from day zero — no parent is signing up for that, and he isn't predicting they will. The real question underneath it is smaller and much closer to home: in the years a teenager is already spending with AI, is it substituting for the humans who should be there, or making room for them to show up better? That's a design question, not a fate — and it's the one this piece has tried to answer at the level of what's happening and why.

The next piece in this series takes the same map into specific, everyday situations — a bullied kid, a stressed one, a curious one — and asks the harder question: when it's midnight and a teenager reaches for their phone, which one should answer?
